newsitem.title: UK: British manufacturing rebounds, services soften.
newsitem.headline: British manufacturing rebounds, services soften.

text.p: British manufacturing output rebounded in June but the services sector, the main engine of the country's economic boom, grew at a slightly slower rate in July, data on Tuesday showed. Economists said the figures did not significantly alter the background for this week's meeting of the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, but the slight softening in services could allow the committee to delay any further interest rate rises.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said manufacturing output rose 0.4 percent in June after an unexpected fall of one percent in May, and was up 1.2 percent year-on-year.
Overall industrial production was up 1.4 percent in June, way above market forecasts of a 0.5 percent rise, and expanded 1.9 percent year-on-year.
Separately, the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply said in its July survey on the services sector that the strong pound was starting to hurt service providers as well as manufacturers.
Its monthly survey, sponsored by Reuters, showed the service sector continued to grow strongly but at a less vigorous pace than in recent months.
Jonathan Loynes, an economist at HSBC, said the strength in overall industrial production reflected a rebound in both energy extraction and supply, but the picture in manufacturing remained weak.

"With the latest survey evidence giving clear evidence that the strength of the pound is hurting, there is a real risk of a further fall in output in the third quarter, putting manufacturing technically back into recession," he said.

Loynes said he expected the monetary policy committee to concentrate more on the strength of services and raise interest rates for the fourth time in as many months. Official interest rates are now at 6.75 percent.

However, David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy said the PMI survey showed trade in services was not immune to the damaging effect of the strong pound. "As time goes on, there are also likely to be spill-over effects from a slowdown in manufacturing," he said. "If this survey does indeed herald the start of a period of more subdued growth in services, then some of the more pessimistic forecasts for UK interest rates could well prove misplaced."
